Rashi on Nazir 41b:1:1.hebrew: ואי כתב רחמנא ראשו ולא כתב זקנו ה"א - דהאי דכתיב "ראשו" תרתי משמע: דאתי עשה דמצורע — דכתיב "וגילח את כל שערו" — ודחי לא תעשה ד"לא תקיפו את פאת ראשכם", ומשמע נמי מדכתיב "לא תקיפו פאת ראשכם", דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה. אבל עדיין לא מצינו דבתער הוי. להכי כתב רחמנא "זקנו", למילף ליה מ"פאת זקנם לא יגלחו", דכתיב ביה השחתה [וגילוח], דהיינו תער:
Rashi on Nazir 41b:1:1.english: And had the Merciful One written “his head” and not written “his beard,” I would say - That that which is written: “his head,” implies two things: that the positive [commandment] of a leper — as it is written: “And he shall shave all his hair” — comes and overrides the negative [commandment] of: “You shall not round the corners of your head”; and it also implies, from that which is written: “You shall not round the corner of your head,” that rounding the entire head is called rounding. But we still have not found that it is [done] with a razor. For this [reason], the Merciful One wrote “his beard,” to derive it from: “They shall not shave the corners of their beard,” regarding which destruction [and shaving] is written, which means a razor.

Rashi on Nazir 41b:2:1.hebrew: ור"א דאתי עשה ודחי לא תעשה מנליה - בשלמא לרבנן, דילפי מצורע מזקנו — דבהשחתת זקן אתא ליה עשה ד"וגילח את כל שערו" ודחי ליה ללאו דהשחתת זקן. אלא לר"א, מנא ליה? אי מהשחתת זקן כרבנן — כיון דלר"א לא אתי ליה עשה ד"וגילח את כל שערו" ולידחי לגמרי את לא תעשה דהשחתת זקן, דלדידיה בתער הוא דמישתרי מצורע אבל לא במלקט ורהיטני, לא אתיא ליה עשה בהדיא ודחי ליה לכוליה לא תעשה אלא לפלגא, דבתער מישתרי אבל לא במלקט ורהיטני. ואי מראשו דמצורע, דדחי ליה ראשו דבנזיר — איכא למיפרך: מה לנזיר, שכן ישנו בשאלה! ואי מזקנו דכהן מצורע, דמותר בתער — איכא למיפרך נמי: דמכהן לא ילפינן, שכן לאו שאינו שוה בכל; וכדאמר לקמן בפרק שני נזירין (נזיר דף נח:):
Rashi on Nazir 41b:2:1.english: And Rabbi Eliezer, from where does he [derive] that a positive [commandment] comes and overrides a negative [commandment]? - Granted according to the Rabbis, who derive [the shaving of] a leper from "his beard" — for regarding the destruction of the beard, the positive [commandment], "and he shall shave all his hair," comes and overrides the negative [commandment] against destroying the beard. But according to Rabbi Eliezer, from where does he [derive it]? If [he derives it] from the destruction of the beard like the Rabbis — since according to Rabbi Eliezer, the positive [commandment], "and he shall shave all his hair," does not come and completely override the negative [commandment] against destroying the beard, as according to him, it is [only] with a razor that a leper is permitted [to shave], but not with tweezers or a plane, [and therefore] a positive [commandment] does not come clearly and override an entire negative [commandment], but only half of it, as with a razor it is permitted, but not with tweezers or a plane. And if [he derives it] from "his head" regarding a leper, which overrides [the prohibition regarding] "his head" in the case of a nazirite — one can refute [this]: What [is notable] about a nazirite? That he is subject to absolution [of his vow]! And if from "his beard" regarding a leper who is a priest, who is permitted [to shave] with a razor — one can refute [this] as well: that we do not derive from a priest, as [his is] a negative commandment that does not apply equally to all; and as [the Gemara] states later on in the chapter [entitled] Shenei Nezirim (Nazir 58b):

Rashi on Nazir 41b:2:2.english: He derives it - From that which is taught [in a baraita]: etc.

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:1.hebrew: ואיצטריך למיכתב זקנו [וראשו], דאי כתב רחמנא זקנו ולא כתב ראשו ה"א דהקפת כל הראש [לא שמיה] הקפה - דעיקר איסור הקפה, דכתיב "לא תקיפו פאת", ה"א: היינו דוקא כשנוטל הפאות לבד, כדאמר בעלמא: "איזו היא הקפה? זה המשוה צדעיו לאחורי אזנו ופדחתו". פי': צידעא הוא השער הרבה וגדל סמוך לאזנים, ומאחורי אזניו חלק הוא ואין שם שער, וכן בפדחתו אין שער. וכשנוטל אותם שבצדעיו, דהיינו פאת הראש, ויהיה חלק שער — נמצא שהוא שוה לאחורי אזניו ופדחתו, ובהא כ"ע מודו שהוא בלאו; ופליגי במגלח כל הראש וגם הפאות, דאיכא למ"ד שמה הקפה, ואיכא למ"ד לא שמה הקפה:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:1.english: And it was necessary to write "his beard" [and "his head," for had the Merciful One written "his beard" and not written "his head," I would say that rounding the entire head [is not called] rounding] - For [regarding] the primary prohibition of rounding, of which it is written: "You shall not round the corner of" (Leviticus 19:27), I would say: this is specifically when one removes the corners alone, as [the Gemara] says elsewhere: "What is rounding? This is one who makes his temples level with [the hairless areas] behind his ear and his forehead." Explanation: Tzida is the abundant hair that grows adjacent to the ears; and behind his ears it is smooth and there is no hair there, and likewise on his forehead there is no hair. And when one removes those [hairs] that are on his temples, which are the corner of the head, and it becomes smooth of hair, it turns out that it is level with [the areas] behind his ears and his forehead, and in this [case] everyone agrees that it is [prohibited] by a negative commandment. And they disagree regarding one who shaves the entire head and the corners as well, for there is an authority who holds that it is called rounding, and there is an authority who holds that it is not called rounding.

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:2.hebrew: להכי כתב רחמנא ראשו - לגלות לן דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה; כיון דדחי עשה דוגילח ראשו ללאו דהקפה, ש"מ הקפה היא:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:2.english: For this reason the Merciful One wrote "his head" - To reveal to us that rounding the entire head is called rounding; since the positive commandment of "and he shall shave his head" overrides the prohibition against rounding, learn from this that it is [considered] rounding.

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:3.hebrew: ואי כתב רחמנא ראשו ה"א משמע תרתי - כלומר, אף כי משמע תרתי — דמשמע דעשה דחי לא תעשה, ומשמע נמי דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה — [ואכתי] בתער לא ידעינן שיהא גילוח דמצורע דוקא בתער; שהרי אהקפת פאת ראש חייב אפילו במספרים, שלא בתער, שלא הוזכר תער בקרא, אלא "לא תקיפו" סתמא. כתב רחמנא "זקנו" — מינה דרשי רבנן לעיל דתגלחת דמצורע דוקא בתער. הלכך, צריכי תרתי: "ראשו" ו"זקנו". ואי קשיא לרבנן: היכא דהוא נזיר ומצורע, דאיכא בראשו דנזיר תרי לאוין ועשה — לאו ד"תער לא יעבור", ועשה ד"גידול פרע", ולאו דהקפה — מנא להו לרבנן דדחי עשה דגילוח דמצורע לכל הנהו? וצ"ל: הכל נפקא להו מ"ראשו", דמקרא מלא דבר הכתוב, לא שנא הוא נזיר ולא שנא אינו נזיר. ועוד, כיון דגלי לן ב"זקנו" דדחי עשה דגילוח לאו ועשה דכהנים — לאו דהשחתת זקן ועשה ד"קדושים תהיו" — הוא הדין שידחה ב' לאוין ועשה, דאין סברא להם לחלק בין לאו אחד לשני לאוין. והכי איכא תנא לקמן (נזיר דף נח.) [בגדילים] דלא מפליג בין לאו אחד לשני לאוין. ואע"ג דלאו ועשה [דכהנים] אינו שוה בכל — ה"נ לאו ועשה דנזיר [ולאו] דהקפה אינו שוה בכל, אלא בנזירין, ואנשים לאו דהקפה. ולקמן בפרק שני נזירים (שם) חשיב לאו דנזיר שוה בכל, ועביד צריכותא: דנזיר מכהנים לא אתי — שכן אינו שוה בכל; וכהנים מנזיר לא אתי — שכן ישנו בשאלה. וא"ת לר"א: כיון דמוקי "ראשו" לראשו דנזיר, ולמימר דעשה דגילוח דחי לאו ד"תער לא יעבור" [וגם] עשה ד"גידול פרע", מאי איצטריך תו [זקנו] לר"א, דעשה דגילוח דחי לאו דכהנים דהשחתת זקן [ועשה] ד"קדושים [תהיו]"? תיפוק ליה מ"ראשו"! דאיכא למיפרך: מה לראשו דנזיר שכן ישנו בשאלה? ועוד, מה לכהנים שכן ריבה בהן הכתוב מצות יתירות, ולכך לא ידחה עשה דגילוח לאו ועשה דכהנים. וכ"ת: לכתוב "זקנו" ולשתוק מ"ראשו"? — ד"ראשו" איצטריך לר"א לאגמורי לן דמצות גילוח דמצורע הוי דוקא בתער, ולא בשאר משחיתים, כדאמר לעיל:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:3.english: “And had the Merciful One written: ‘His head,’ I would say it teaches two” - That is to say: Even though it implies two [matters] — as it implies that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition, and it also implies that rounding the entire head is called rounding — [still], with a razor we would not know that the shaving of a leper must specifically be with a razor; for regarding the rounding of the corner of the head, one is liable even with scissors, without a razor, since a razor is not mentioned in the verse, but rather “You shall not round” (Leviticus 19:27) generically. The Merciful One [therefore] wrote “his beard” (Leviticus 14:9) — from it the Rabbis derived above (40b) that the shaving of a leper is specifically with a razor. Therefore, both are necessary: “his head” and “his beard.” And if it is difficult according to the Rabbis: Where he is [both] a nazirite and a leper, such that there are on the head of a nazirite two prohibitions and a positive commandment — the prohibition of “a razor shall not pass [over his head]” (Numbers 6:5), the positive commandment of letting the locks of hair grow long [gidul pera] (ibid.), and the prohibition of rounding [the corners of the head] (Leviticus 19:27) — from where do the Rabbis derive that the positive commandment of a leper's shaving overrides all of these? And one must say: They derive it all from “his head,” for the verse spoke comprehensively, whether he is a nazirite or whether he is not a nazirite. And furthermore: Since [the Torah] revealed to us regarding “his beard” that the positive commandment of shaving overrides the prohibition and positive commandment of priests — the prohibition against destroying the beard (Leviticus 21:5) and the positive commandment of “They shall be holy” (Leviticus 21:6) — the same applies that it should override two prohibitions and a positive commandment, as they have no reason to distinguish between one prohibition and two prohibitions. And so there is a Tanna later (Nazir 58a) [regarding ritual fringes (gedilim)] who does not distinguish between one prohibition and two prohibitions. And even though the prohibition and positive commandment [of priests] do not apply equally to all, so too the prohibition and positive commandment of a nazirite and the prohibition of rounding do not apply equally to all, but rather [only] to nazirites, and [to] men — the prohibition of rounding. And later, in the chapter [entitled] “Shnei Nezirin” (ibid.), [the Gemara] considers the prohibition of a nazirite to apply equally to all, and formulates a necessity [for both verses]: that a nazirite cannot be derived from priests, as [the prohibition of priests] does not apply equally to all; and priests cannot be derived from a nazirite, as [the nazirite vow] is subject to dissolution [by halakhic inquiry]. And if you should say: According to Rabbi Eliezer, since he establishes “his head” [as referring] to the head of a nazirite, to teach that the positive commandment of shaving overrides the prohibition of “a razor shall not pass” [and also] the positive commandment of letting the locks of hair grow long, why was [“his beard”] further necessary according to Rabbi Eliezer, [to teach] that the positive commandment of shaving overrides the prohibition of priests against destroying the beard [and the positive commandment] of “They shall be [holy]”? Let him derive it from “his head”! [One can answer] that one could refute [such a derivation]: What [is notable] about the head of a nazirite? It is that [his vow] is subject to dissolution. And furthermore: What [is notable] about priests? It is that the verse amplified additional mitzvot for them; and therefore the positive commandment of shaving would not override the prohibition and positive commandment of priests [without an explicit verse]. And if you should say: Let [the Torah] write “his beard” and remain silent regarding “his head”? — [That cannot be, for] “his head” was necessary according to Rabbi Eliezer to teach us that the mitzva of a leper's shaving is specifically with a razor, and not with other destroying implements, as [the Gemara] said above.

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:4.hebrew: השתא (פ"ק) משמע הכא בסוגיא דידן דהקפת הראש הוי אפילו בלא תער. וכן איתא בת"כ: "זאת תהיה תורת המצורע... ראשו" — מה ת"ל? לפי שיש בזקן משא"כ בראש, ובראש משא"כ בזקן: שהראש אסור במספרים, והזקן מותר. והא דתניא בתוספתא (דמכות פ"ג): "חייב שתים, אחת לצידעא מכאן ואחת לצידעא מכאן, ואינו חייב עד שיקיפנו בתער" — היינו כעין תער. ובמכות (דף כ:) נמי דקאמר: "משוה צידעיו לאחורי אזנו ופדחתו" — נמי היינו כעין תער, ואפילו במספרים. וההיא דת"כ איכא למדחי, דע"כ לאו באיסור הקפת הראש מיירי, אלא בנזיר, דאסור לגלח ראשו תוך ימי נזרו, ואף במספרים, למ"ד לעיל לרבות כל מעבירין. והכי מוכחא סיפא דהתם, דתנא בו: "והראש מותר לכל אדם והזקן אסור לכל אדם"; ואי בהקפת הראש איירי, איך מותר ראש בכל אדם? אלמא בנזיר מיירי, וקאמר דתגלחת אינו מותר בכל אדם, שאינם נזירין. ומיהו צריך ליזהר שלא ליטול פאת הראש אפילו במספרים, דשפיר איקרו כעין תער; וכן נהגו העולם כשמגלחין התינוקות, לשייר בצדעיהן הרבה שערות:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:1:4.english: Now (in the first chapter [of Yevamot]), it is implied here in our sugya that rounding of the head is [forbidden] even without a razor. And so it is stated in Torat Kohanim: “This shall be the law of the leper... his head” (Leviticus 14:9) — why does the verse state [this]? Because there is [a stringency] in the beard that is not in the head, and in the head that is not in the beard: for [shaving] the head is forbidden with scissors, whereas [shaving] the beard is permitted [with scissors]. And that which is taught in the Tosefta (Makkot, ch. 3): “He is liable for two [sets of lashes], one for the temple on this side and one for the temple on that side, and he is not liable until he rounds it with a razor” — that means [with scissors cutting] like a razor. And in Makkot (20b) as well, where it says: “One who levels his temples to the back of his ear and [to] his forehead” — that too means like a razor, and [it means] even with scissors [cutting close like a razor]. And that [teaching] of Torat Kohanim can be refuted [and reinterpreted]: that of necessity, it is not dealing with the prohibition of rounding the head, but rather with a nazirite, who is forbidden to shave his head during the days of his naziriteship, and even with scissors according to the one who said above (39b) [that the verse serves] to include all hair removers. And so the latter clause there proves, where it taught: “and [shaving] the head is permitted to everyone, whereas [shaving] the beard is forbidden to everyone.” And if it were dealing with rounding the head, how could [shaving] the head be permitted to everyone? Rather, it is evident that it is dealing with a nazirite, and it means that [such] shaving is not permitted to everyone, [except to those] who are not nazirites. Nevertheless, one must be careful not to remove the corner of the head [the peyot] even with scissors, for they may well be called “like a razor” [when cut close to the skin]. And so is the custom of the world when they cut the hair of young children, to leave many hairs on their temples.

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:2:1.hebrew: ור"א דאתי עשה ודחי לא תעשה מנא ליה - וא"ת: וליתי מראשו וזקנו, דדחי עשה אפילו לאו ועשה! וכ"ת: דמה להנך שכן לאו שאינו שוה בכל הוא, דלאו דזקנו ליתא בנשים, כדאמר פ"ק דקידושין (דף לה:) — א"כ, גם לרבנן תיקשה: מנלן דבעלמא עשה דחי לא תעשה? ואומר הר"ף: דמש"ה פריך לר"א, דמוקי להאי ראשו משום נזיר, דאיכא לאו ועשה, וא"כ [צריך] מקרא אחרינא; דאל"כ, לא מצי לאוקמי לקרא דראשו ללא תעשה ועשה, אלא בלאו גרידא ובראשו דאיניש דעלמא, למידחי לאו דהקפה, כמו שרבנן מעמידין אותו לאשמועינן דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה, וזקנו לאשמועינן דאפילו לאו ועשה דחי; ואי לא הוה [כתיב ראשו לא הוי] ידעינן דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה, קמ"ל ראשו. ובתוספות אחרינא מפרש הכי: לר"א, עשה דדחי לא תעשה מנא ליה? מדמוקי זקנו לעיל בכהן מצורע, ודחי עשה דגילוח לאו ועשה דכהנים — לאו דזקן ועשה דקדושים תהיו — אלמא פשיטא ליה לר"א בעלמא דעשה דחי לאו גרידא; דאל"כ, מנא ליה לאוקמיה בכהן? לוקמיה בזקן דישראל דמצורע, ולאשמועינן דעשה דגילוח דמצורע דחי לאו דהשחתה דישראל, אבל בכהן מצורע דלמא לא דחי לאו ועשה דכהנים דקדושים! דבשלמא לרבנן, דמוקמי ראשו דמצורע למימר דעשה דגילוח דחי לאו דהקפת הראש, א"כ ה"ה דעשה דמצורע דחי לאו דפאת זקן, והלכך לישראל וכו'. והר"ם אמר: דלרבנן ניחא, דמצינו למימר דראשו, אם אינו ענין לשאינו שוה בכל — דנפקא לן מזקנו, אפילו לאו ועשה שאינו שוה בכל — תניהו ענין ללאו השוה בכל. ואל תתמה: דהלא שפיר אצטריך ראשו לאשמועינן דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה? דאיכא למימר: [מסברא] נפקא ליה. וכזה תמצא הסוגיא חלוקה ריש שני נזירין (לקמן נזיר דף נח. ושם): דמעיקרא בעי הש"ס למימר דמוקי ראשו להקפת ראש גרידא, לאשמועינן דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה; ובתר הכי צ"ל בכלל הסוגיא דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה, לרווחא דמלתא אמרה הש"ס הכי: את"ל דשפיר נפקא לן דעשה דוחה לא תעשה מגדילים אכלאים [אתי ואי] אתי גדילים לכדרבא, כדאמר במסכת יבמות (דף ד:), שקיל הש"ס: דהא לרבנן שפיר נפקא דעשה דוחה לא תעשה באם אינו ענין, ואז נאמר דהקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה, כדמסיק ריש פרק שני נזירין. אבל לר"א, דמוקי ראשו לנזיר מצורע, וגם זקנו אתא לכהן — אי גמרינן מנייהו, נאמר דפליגי דעשה דוחה לא תעשה ועשה; אבל לר"א צ"ל ע"כ דנפקא ליה דעשה דוחה ל"ת גרידא בכל לאו כהאי, דאי לא, תער מנא ליה במצורע? דאי מראשו, דלמא לאו למדחי נזיר דאית ביה תרי לאוי, דהקפת דנזיר, אלא לאו דהקפה גרידא! אלא דס"ל השתא להש"ס דפליג ר"א [ואמר]: הקפת כל הראש לא שמה הקפה; אלא משום דאיכא למפרך, כדפרישית בריש מסכת יבמות (דף ה. ושם): מה לכהן שכן אינו שוה בכל? נזיר יוכיח. מה לנזיר שכן ישנו בשאלה? ואיצטריך תרוייהו, ואכתי: דעשה דחי לא תעשה השוה בכל מנליה:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:2:1.english: And Rabbi Eliezer, from where does he derive that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition? — And if you say: Let him derive [it] from "his head" and "his beard" [regarding a person afflicted with tzara'at], where a positive commandment overrides even a prohibition and a positive commandment! And if you say: What [is unique] about these is that it is a prohibition that does not apply equally to everyone, for the prohibition of [shaving] one's beard does not apply to women, as [the Gemara] states in the first chapter of Kiddushin (35b) — if so, for the Rabbis as well, the question should be difficult: From where do we [derive] that in general a positive commandment overrides a prohibition? And the Rav Porat says: That for this reason [the Gemara] poses the challenge to Rabbi Eliezer, because he interprets this verse of "his head" regarding a nazirite, where there is both a prohibition and a positive commandment. And if so, another verse is [needed]; for otherwise, he could not interpret the verse of "his head" regarding a prohibition and a positive commandment, but rather regarding an ordinary prohibition, and on the head of an ordinary person, to override the prohibition against rounding [the corners of the head], as the Rabbis interpret it to teach us that rounding the entire head is called rounding, while "his beard" comes to teach us that [a positive commandment] overrides even a prohibition and a positive commandment; and had ["his head" not been written, we would not have] known that rounding the entire head is called rounding, so ["his head"] teaches us this. And in another Tosafot it is explained as follows: According to Rabbi Eliezer, from where does he derive that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition? Since above he interprets "his beard" regarding a priest afflicted with tzara'at, where the positive commandment of shaving overrides both the prohibition and positive commandment of priests — the prohibition regarding the beard and the positive commandment of "They shall be holy" — evidently it is obvious to Rabbi Eliezer that in general a positive commandment overrides an ordinary prohibition. For if that were not so, from where does he know to interpret it regarding a priest? Let him interpret it regarding the beard of an ordinary Israelite afflicted with tzara'at, to teach us that the positive commandment of shaving for a person with tzara'at overrides the prohibition against shaving the corners of the beard for an Israelite; whereas regarding a priest afflicted with tzara'at, perhaps [the positive commandment] would not override the prohibition and positive commandment of priests of "They shall be holy"! For it is understandable according to the Rabbis, who interpret "his head" of a person with tzara'at to mean that the positive commandment of shaving overrides the prohibition against rounding the head; if so, the same principle applies that the [positive commandment of] shaving of a person with tzara'at overrides the prohibition of the corner of the beard, and therefore for an Israelite, etc. And the Ram [Rabbeinu Meir] said that according to the Rabbis it is resolved, because we can say that regarding "his head," if it is not needed for a matter that does not apply equally to all — which we derive from "his beard," even for a prohibition and a positive commandment that does not apply equally to all — apply it to a matter regarding a prohibition that applies equally to all. And do not wonder: "Behold, was not 'his head' rightly needed to teach us that rounding the entire head is called rounding?" — for it can be said that he derives this [from logic]. And similarly, you will find the discussion divided at the beginning of [the chapter] Shenei Nezirim (below, Nazir 58a and there): Initially, the Talmud seeks to say that he interprets "his head" for rounding the head alone, to teach us that rounding the entire head is called rounding; and subsequently, it must be said in the broader scope of the discussion that [the statement that] rounding the entire head is called rounding was stated by the Talmud merely as an additional consideration, [meaning]: "If you wish to say that it is well derived that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition from fringes on diverse kinds, [this is resolved; and if] fringes is needed for that which Rava taught, as [the Gemara] states in tractate Yevamot (4b)," the Talmud deliberates that for the Rabbis, it is indeed well derived that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition through "if it is not needed," and then we say that rounding the entire head is called rounding, as is concluded at the beginning of chapter Shenei Nezirim. However, according to Rabbi Eliezer, who interprets "his head" for a nazirite afflicted with tzara'at, and "his beard" also comes for a priest: if we were to derive from them, we would say that they differ, [holding] that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition and a positive commandment; but according to Rabbi Eliezer, one must say perforce that he derives that a positive commandment overrides an ordinary prohibition in every such prohibition. For if not, from where does he know that a razor [is required] for a person afflicted with tzara'at? For if from "his head," perhaps [it does] not come to override [the restrictions of] a nazirite, in which there are two prohibitions: of rounding [and] of a nazirite, but rather an ordinary prohibition of rounding alone! Rather, the Talmud now maintains that Rabbi Eliezer disagrees [and maintains that] rounding the entire head is not called rounding; but rather because [the derivation] can be refuted, as I explained at the beginning of tractate Yevamot (5a and there): What [is unique] about a priest? That [his prohibition] does not apply equally to all. A nazirite will prove [otherwise]. What [is unique] about a nazirite? That his vow is subject to absolution. And both were necessary. And still, from where does he derive that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition that applies equally to all?

Tosafot on Nazir 41b:2:2.hebrew: יליף מגדילים - דסמכיה רחמנא ציצית לכלאים למימר דעשה דציצית דחי לא תעשה דכלאים. ובהכי ניחא: בריש מסכת דיבמות לא מצי הש"ס למיפשט דעשה דוחה לא תעשה גרידא השוה בכל מראשו וזקנו, והכא פשיטא לרבנן דדחי בלא גדילים? והשתא ניחא ליה, דסוגיא דשמעתין דיבמות דבעי למימר דאיצטריך קרא לראשו דהקפת ראש שמה הקפה, ולהכי ליכא לאוכוחי דעשה דוחה לא תעשה באם אינו ענין; [אבל] ריש סוגיא דפרק שני נזירין סבר: הקפת כל הראש שמה הקפה מסברא:
Tosafot on Nazir 41b:2:2.english: He derives [it] from "twisted cords" - For the Merciful One juxtaposed ritual fringes to forbidden mixtures, to say that the positive commandment of ritual fringes overrides the negative commandment of forbidden mixtures. And through this, [the following question] is resolved: At the beginning of tractate Yevamot, the Shas was unable to resolve that a positive commandment overrides a mere negative commandment that applies equally to all from "his head" and "his beard," whereas here it is obvious to the Rabbis that it overrides [even] without "twisted cords"? And now it is resolved for him: for the sugya of the passage in Yevamot wanted to say that the verse was necessary for "his head" [to teach] that rounding the head is considered rounding, and for this reason one cannot prove that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment through [the principle of] "if it is not relevant [to its own topic, apply it to another]"; [whereas] the beginning of the sugya of the chapter [entitled] Shenei Nezirim holds [that] rounding the entire head is considered rounding based on logic.
